The **Academy Award for Best Director** (officially known as the **Academy Award of Merit for Directing**) is an award presented annually by the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") (AMPAS). It is given in honor of a [film director](/wiki/Film_director "Film director") who has exhibited outstanding directing while working in the [film industry](/wiki/Film_industry "Film industry").

The [1st Academy Awards](/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") ceremony was held in 1929 with the award being split into "Dramatic" and "Comedy" categories; [Frank Borzage](/wiki/Frank_Borzage "Frank Borzage") and [Lewis Milestone](/wiki/Lewis_Milestone "Lewis Milestone") won for *[7th Heaven](/wiki/7th_Heaven_(1927_film) "7th Heaven (1927 film)")* and *[Two Arabian Knights](/wiki/Two_Arabian_Knights "Two Arabian Knights")*, respectively.[[1]](#cite_note-1) However, these categories were merged for all subsequent ceremonies.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Nominees are determined by [single transferable vote](/wiki/Single_transferable_

The waters of the Nile originate as rainfall in the mountains in the south and east regions of the Nile Basin.

The Nile is a major river in northeast Africa which flows into the Mediterranean Sea. The Nile Basin is [all land that drains](/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") into the Nile, and it covers 2,927,843 km2 – about 10% of the African continent (see adjacent map).[[6]](#cite_note-basinSize-8) Eleven countries are wholly or partially within the basin: Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Sudan, Tanzania, and Uganda.[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllan2009753-39)[[j]](#cite_note-41) The basin covers a wide variety of climates, ecosystems, and topographies – ranging from arid, sandy deserts in the north, to flat, swampy wetlands in the middle, to rainy, forested mountains in the south.[[32]](#cite_note-42)

The basin can be divided into seven regions; five of these regions encompass the longest course of the Nile. Proceeding in a downstream sequence, these five regions are: the [African Great Lakes](/wiki/African_Great_Lakes "African Great Lakes"), the [Mountain Nile](/wiki/Mountain_Nile "Mountain Nile"), the [White Nile](/wiki/White_Nile "White Nile"), the main Nile, and the [Nile Delta](/wiki/Nile_Delta "Nile Delta"). Two additional regions encompass major tributaries: the [Blue Nile](/wiki/Blue_Nile "Blue Nile") and the [Atbarah River](/wiki/Atbarah_River "Atbarah River").[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurst2025-12)

Greater warming increases the amount of moisture in the atmosphere over Asia, which directly leads to extreme precipitation. Probability of 20-year, 50-year and 100-year extremes consistently increases with warming across Asia. In the most affected parts of South Asia, up to a 15-fold average increase for 100-year extremes is possible under 3 °C (5.4 °F) of warming.[[202]](#cite_note-Guo2023-209)

South Asian countries are expected to experience more flooding in the future as the monsoon pattern intensifies.[[203]](#cite_note-AR6_WGII_Chapter10-210): 1459 Across Asia as a whole, 100-year extremes in vapour transport (directly related to extreme precipitation) would become 2.6 times more frequent under 1.5 °C (2.7 °F) of global warming, yet 3.9 and 7.5 times more frequent under 2 °C (3.6 °F) and 3 °C (5.4 °F). In parts of South Asia, they could become up to 15 times more frequent.[[202]](#cite_note-Guo2023-209) At the same time, up to two-thirds of glacier ice in the Hindu Kush region may melt by 2100 under high warming, and these glaciers feed the water basin of over 220 million people.[[203]](#cite_note-AR6_WGII_Chapter10-210): 1487 As glacier meltwater flow diminishes after 2050, [Hydropower](/wiki/Hydropower "Hydropower") generation would become less predictable and reliable, while agriculture would become more reliant on the intensified monsoon than ever before.[[204]](#cite_note-:HKH2019Climate-211)[[205]](#cite_note-:HKH2019Cryo-212)[[206]](#cite_note-:HKH2019Water-213) Around 2050, people living in the [Ganges](/wiki/Ganges "Ganges") and [Indus](/wiki/Indus "Indus") river basins (where up to 60% of non-monsoon irrigation comes from the glaciers[[207]](#cite_note-Biemans2019-214)) may be faced with severe water scarcity due to both climate and socioeconomic reasons.[[203]](#cite_note-AR6_WGII_Chapter10-210): 1486

Fudan became a private university in 1917, establishing specialised departments including Chinese literature, foreign literature, banking, business and administration, economics, politics, civil engineering and psychology.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4): 63 In 1921, university preparatory education was ended and the university began to adopt an American-styled credit and elective system, per a national policy.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4): 69 In 1928, Fudan was registered with the Ministry of Education of the newly founded Nationalist government. In 1929, the university was organised into four faculties, namely Liberal Arts, Science, Law and Commerce. In 1937, it moved to Chongqing due to the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4): 71

In 1941, with the approval from the Nationalist government, the university was transformed from a private university to a national university, which allowed the government to control Fudan's major posts, including the president, provost and dean. In early 1946, the university returned to Shanghai.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4): 71 In China under Chiang Kai-shek and the Kuomintang, Fudan University was tasked with providing a Western-style education to Chinese students to support the country's economic reconstruction efforts.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4): 75

Shortly after its discovery, Neptune was referred to simply as "the planet exterior to Uranus" or as "Le Verrier's planet". The first suggestion for a name came from Galle, who proposed the name *[Janus](/wiki/Janus_(mythology) "Janus (mythology)")*. In England, Challis put forward the name *[Oceanus](/wiki/Oceanus "Oceanus")*.[[50]](#cite_note-55)

Claiming the right to name his discovery, Le Verrier quickly proposed the name *Neptune* for this new planet, though falsely stating that this had been officially approved by the French [Bureau des Longitudes](/wiki/Bureau_des_Longitudes "Bureau des Longitudes").[[51]](#cite_note-56) In October, he sought to name the planet *Le Verrier*, after himself, and he had loyal support in this from the observatory director, [François Arago](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Arago "François Arago"). This suggestion met with stiff resistance outside France.[[52]](#cite_note-57) French almanacs quickly reintroduced the name *Herschel* for Uranus, after that planet's discoverer Sir [William Herschel](/wiki/William_Herschel "William Herschel"), and *Leverrier* for the new planet.[[53]](#cite_note-58)

[Struve](/wiki/Friedrich_Georg_Wilhelm_von_Struve "Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve") came out in favour of the name *Neptune* on 29 December 1846, to the [Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Russian_Academy_of_Sciences "Russian Academy of Sciences"),[[54]](#cite_note-59) after the colour of the planet as viewed through a telescope.[[55]](#cite_note-60) Soon, *Neptune* became the internationally accepted name. In [Roman mythology](/wiki/Roman_mythology "Roman mythology"), [Neptune](/wiki/Neptune_(mythology) "Neptune (mythology)") was the god of the sea, identified with the Greek [Poseidon](/wiki/Poseidon "Poseidon"). The demand for a mythological name seemed to be in keeping with the nomenclature of the other planets, all of which were named for deities in [Greek](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") and Roman mythology.[[f]](#cite_note-61)[[56]](#cite_note-USGS-62)
